When a mobile terminal takes part in over-the-air training, its own motion rotates the gradient that travels back through it; a movable antenna that keeps pace with the terminal rotates it back---without any channel estimate. We give a speed law: under a scalar conditional-mean model of the physical return, landing the residual displacement inside the first positive lobe of the spatial correlation keeps the conditional mean gradient a descent direction, which, given sufficient travel, fixes a critical actuator-to-terminal speed ratio. We further prove a bias--jitter law: under the same scalar conditional-mean model and with zero effective bias, independent zero-mean Gaussian jitter of any finite amplitude scales the conditional mean gradient without reversing its direction, whereas a sub-wavelength systematic bias can reverse it. This result motivates prioritizing bias calibration to preserve gradient direction. Simulations on 3GPP CDL-A channels show that an antenna keeping pace with the terminal achieves near-CSI accuracy without digital channel correction, reaching 98.58 % compared with 98.59% for the ideal-CSI reference. The simulations also show that partial compensation can support learning when the residual displacement falls within a later positive correlation lobe, so a faster actuator does not necessarily yield higher accuracy. Separate positioning simulations show a sharp accuracy loss under systematic bias but little degradation under zero-mean Gaussian jitter of comparable spatial scale.
Degenerated scalar balance laws: stability of the critical wave

We consider scalar balance laws whith degenerated growth function at one infinity. It is the transition point between monostable and bistable waves. We find it admits smooth profiles arising from both settings, and show stability for the slowest of these waves, under a sign assumption on the flux. The presence of a characteristic point at infinity weaken the temporal decay: an exponential spatial localization loss is necessary to get algebraic temporal decay.
Linearization in nonlocal elasticity via Gamma-convergence
Carolin Kreisbeck; Carlos Mora-Corral; Felix Seifert

Linearization is a classical tool in continuum mechanics that connects nonlinear models of solids to their linear counterparts through the small-strain limit, as in the passage from finite to linear elasticity. Here, we study a nonlocal analogue of this limit process in the context of state-based peridynamics, starting from a class of models in nonlocal hyperelasticity subject to nonlocal Dirichlet boundary conditions. Recent formal calculations in the literature indicate that the linearized versions of these models are closely related to the widely used Eringen models. The main purpose of this note is to make this connection rigorous by establishing $Γ$-convergence of the associated energy functionals and a corresponding compactness result that together imply strong convergence of minimizers. Our proof relies on a local-to-nonlocal transfer argument that reduces the problem to a well-known local linearization result.
Regularising Flows and Singular Fractional SDEs with Superlinear Dissipation

We study stochastic differential equations driven by the fractional Riemann-Liouville process with Hurst parameter $H\in(0,1)$, whose drift is the sum of a possibly distributional vector field $b$ and a smooth, one-sided Lipschitz, dissipative vector field $F$ with coercivity of order $k+1$ and polynomially growing derivatives. If $b \in \mathcal{C}^γ(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$ for some $γ<1$ satisfying $γ>\max\{1-1/(2H),2-1/H\}$, and if $H+1/(k-1)>(1-γ)H/2$, we construct a solution by smooth approximation and prove uniqueness in a class defined through local comparison with the flow generated by the dissipative drift. Watanabe's Learning Coefficients in Item Response Theory
Joe Suzuki; Takumi Ikejiri; Yuki Kurumadani

We study the joint-parameter two-parameter logistic (2PL) model in item response theory, in which both item parameters and respondent abilities are treated as unknown fixed parameters. We first characterize its singular structure through the Fisher information matrix. The parameterization has an inherent scale indeterminacy; when all discrimination parameters are nonzero and the ability parameters are not all equal, its tangent direction is the only null direction and the quotient model is locally regular. We then classify the additional rank deficiencies caused by zero discrimination parameters and degenerate ability configurations. This classification separates the strata governed by a nondegenerate quadratic approximation from those requiring an analysis of higher-order product singularities. Under an asymptotic regime in which the numbers of items and respondents are fixed and the number of independent response matrices tends to infinity, we derive explicit local and global learning coefficients and multiplicities for every realizable true response distribution. The global formulas depend only on the true response probabilities, including cases in which some probabilities equal \(1/2\) or are constant across respondents. These results extend previous calculations restricted to nonzero true discrimination parameters and provide the quantities required for applying sBIC to the joint-parameter 2PL model. Comparing word probabilities in finite groups

We use results from extremal graph theory and analysis to compare word probabilities in finite groups. In particular, we show that the probability of satisfying the 2-Engel word admits a positive lower bound in terms of the probability that an element has order dividing 3. More generally, using a group removal lemma, we obtain analogous bounds for $x^m$-good words.
Time-optimal vaccination in state-dependent SIR models: a single switch criterion and numerical examples outside its regime

In a susceptible, infected, and recovered (SIR) model with constant rates, a time-optimal vaccination policy has at most one switch from no vaccination to maximal vaccination. If $β+I\partial_Iβ>0$ and $G:=\partial_S(βS-γ)>0$ throughout the forward invariant state space, then every optimal control is bang-bang with at most one switch. The incidence condition allows the transmission coefficient to decrease with prevalence. The Pontryagin analysis shows that $G$, the sensitivity of per capita infected growth to the susceptible fraction, and the infected costate together determine the crossing direction of the switching function. We also prove existence of an optimal control, derive explicit a priori upper bounds on the eradication time and characterize the switching time by an optimization over one variable. For parameter sets that violate $G>0$, numerical optimization gives controls with two switches and smaller eradication times than the computed minima over the single switch family. Global well-posedness for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations in 3D bounded domains under a new smallness condition

We investigate the three-dimensional barotropic compressible Navier--Stokes equations involving vacuum in a bounded domain with Navier-slip boundary conditions. It is shown that such a model admits a unique global strong solution provided the gradient of the initial velocity and the initial pressure deviation are suitably small in $L^2$. In particular, \textit{the smallness threshold depends only on the known parameters and the prescribed density bounds.} Our result provides a new analytical framework for the global well-posedness theory of the compressible Navier--Stokes equations.

Zihao Li; Shota Deguchi; Mitsuteru Asai; Shunhua Chen; Naoto Mitsume

Predicting the drag coefficient $C_\mathrm{d}$ of irregular particles requires representing their complex three-dimensional geometry in a form suitable for predictive models. Empirical drag correlations and many data-driven models represent particle geometry through a small set of hand-crafted shape descriptors. When the evaluated geometric variations are represented in the training data, the two learned models achieve comparable accuracy for regular ellipsoids, while VAE-MLP yields lower errors for irregular particles. At the strongest tested perturbation, the mean errors across these runs are 4.97% for VAE-MLP and 9.88% for Descriptor-MLP. Covert Digital Semantic Communication With Movable Antennas: Constellation Shaping, Spatial Optimization, and Semantic Mapping

Digital semantic communication (SemCom) is emerging as a bandwidth-efficient paradigm for next-generation wireless networks by delivering the meaning of a source over finite constellations. However, the broadcast nature of wireless channels exposes transmissions to adversarial wardens, while discrete symbols deviate from the Gaussian signaling assumed by conventional covert communication. In this paper, we propose a covert digital SemCom system assisted by movable antennas (MAs), where the constellation, the antenna positions, and the semantic transceiver are jointly designed to conceal the transmission while preserving the semantic fidelity. Specifically, the maximum covert rate against the optimal detector with unknown noise level is derived in closed-form, which reveals that the legitimate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scales with the moment-matching order of the constellation and the spatial gain provided by the MA array. A Gauss-Laguerre ring constellation is then designed to raise the moment-matching order under the peak power constraints, and a covert symbol mapping with rank-to-ring assignment and scrambling is developed to carry the semantics in the ordering of the latent magnitudes. Guided by the derived semantic distortion bound, the semantic encoder and decoder are trained end-to-end through an invertible flow over the designed constellation and MA array. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme supports a higher achievable covert rate and improves the reconstruction quality by 24% compared to state-of-the-art SemCom schemes.

Mobility in three-dimensional (3D) cellular networks induces frequent handovers and random sojourn times for aerial users. Analyzing these events is challenging because they jointly depend on user trajectories and random service-boundary geometry. This paper develops a unified geometric--kinematic framework in which service regions form a stationary random tessellation, their boundaries constitute a random closed set, and user motion follows a cruise--turn mobility model. Under the stated stationarity, isotropy, and independence conditions, the handover rate satisfies the exact law \(H=(S_V/2)\bar v\), where \(S_V\) is the specific surface area and \(\bar v\) is the long-run mean speed. The forward boundary-distance distribution provides the local geometric input to an effective-traversal approximation for the mean remaining sojourn time. These results link global and local geometric descriptors to complementary mobility metrics. Combining the handover law with link coverage yields a handover-aware effective spectral efficiency for base station (BS) density selection and service-architecture comparison. We then specialize the framework to Poisson--Voronoi single-BS service and Poisson--Delaunay four-BS coordinated multi-point service; under both models, the handover rate scales as \(λ^{1/3}\bar v\). Numerical results corroborate the exact handover expressions, assess the sojourn-time approximations, and show how user speed and interruption duration affect the preferred density and architecture.
Juncheng Wei; Zetian Yan; Zikai Ye

We prove sharp improved Sobolev inequalities on $\mathbb{S}^n$, $n\ge 4$, for functions whose critical density $|u|^{2n/(n-2)}$ has zero barycenter, without any symmetry assumption. The Dirichlet coefficient improves by the optimal factor $2^{-2/n}$, while the coefficient of the $L^2$ term remains one. Equality holds precisely for constant functions. This establishes the sharp form of Aubin's improved Sobolev inequality in every dimension $n\ge4$.
